# Intervals & Sweep Line {#sec-int} ::: {.callout-note title="Sources"} **CLRS** (3rd ed.) § 16.1 (activity selection, the greedy choice and its exchange argument) · **Erickson** *Algorithms* ch. 4 (greedy algorithms; scheduling classes and the "greedy stays ahead" proof) · **CPH** (Laaksonen) ch. 6 (greedy scheduling) and ch. 30 (sweep line algorithms) · **Kleinberg–Tardos** § 4.1 (interval scheduling and interval partitioning: the peak overlap equals the number of rooms) · **Wikipedia**: interval scheduling, interval graph, sweep line algorithm · **Problem statements** of the fourteen problems solved here (LeetCode, Codeforces, CSES), which reduce to the five moves this chapter names. ::: ::: {.callout-tip title="What you will be able to do"} - State an **endpoint convention** (closed, half-open, open) for every interval problem, write the overlap test for it, and choose the event tie-breaker at equal coordinates that matches it. - **Merge** a family of intervals in $O(n\log n)$ with one sort by start and a running block end, **insert** into a merged list in $O(n)$, and read off **gaps** and **union length** from the same walk. - Turn intervals into **$+1$/$-1$ events** and sweep them to get the peak overlap, the time above a capacity, the union length, and the **number of rooms** needed, which equals the peak. - Pick the right greedy among three: **pack** (sort by end, maximum disjoint intervals), **stab** (sort by end, fewest points hitting all), **cover** (sort by start, fewest intervals covering a segment), and prove each with an exchange argument. - Intersect two sorted interval lists with **two pointers**, intersect a whole family with $[\max l, \min r]$, and know where greedy stops: intervals on a **circle** need a split, intervals with **weights** need DP. ::: ## Why this matters {#sec-int-why} ::: {.callout-note title="In plain words"} An interval is **a piece of a line**: $[a, b]$, "everything from $a$ to $b$". A meeting, a reservation, a film, a trip in a car, a balloon on the $x$-axis, a range of days: each is an interval, and the questions are always about how the pieces sit relative to each other. Do they overlap? How many overlap at the worst moment? How many can I keep without clashes? How few points touch them all? Where are the holes? Draw the intervals as horizontal bars on one timeline (@fig-int-idea) and every question becomes a walk from left to right. ::: The tools are ones you already own. Sorting buys a monotone order to walk in (@sec-srt); the difference array and its sparse form, the event sweep, count how many ranges cover each point (@sec-pref-diff); binary search counts how many starts or ends lie left of a point (@sec-bst); and two pointers walk two sorted lists at once (@sec-tp-merge). This chapter spends them on one object, a set of intervals, and shows that nearly every interval problem is **one sort plus one linear pass**, once you choose the right coordinate to sort by and the right rule at equal coordinates. The next chapter, @sec-part, leaves intervals behind and rearranges an array in place. The constraints that point here: $n$ up to $10^5$ or $2 \cdot 10^5$ intervals, coordinates up to $10^9$ (so no array indexed by coordinate), and a question about overlaps, gaps, a schedule or a cover. $O(n^2)$ pairwise checks are then too slow, and $O(n \log n)$ is the target. ::: {#fig-int-idea} ::: {#e6dc6f41 .cell renderings='["light","dark"]' execution_count=2} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](014_intervals_files/figure-html/cell-3-output-1.png){width=451 height=253} ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](014_intervals_files/figure-html/cell-3-output-2.png){width=451 height=253} ::: ::: Four closed intervals as bars on one timeline, and under the axis the number of bars covering each integer point $t = 1, \dots, 9$. The amber cells are the peak, $3$, reached on $[4,5]$. Merging, counting, scheduling and covering all read this one picture; the algorithms differ only in what they track while walking it from left to right. ::: Five lessons build the toolkit, and five patterns spend it: - **A1. The endpoint contract.** Closed $[a,b]$, half-open $[a,b)$, open $(a,b)$: three overlap tests and three tie-breakers when two intervals meet at a point. Pick the wrong one and an answer is off by one exactly on touching inputs. - **A2. Merge after sorting by start.** One pass with a running block end; insertion into an already merged list without sorting; gaps for free. - **A3. Events and the sweep.** Split every interval into $(a, +1)$ and $(b, -1)$, sort, keep a running count: peak overlap, union length, time above a capacity, and the number of rooms needed. - **A4. Three greedies.** Sort by **end** to *pack* the most disjoint intervals, sort by **end** to *stab* all intervals with the fewest points, sort by **start** to *cover* a segment with the fewest intervals. Each has a two-line exchange proof, and each fails with the other sort. - **A5. Where the line breaks.** Intervals on a **circle** (split at the cut) and intervals with **weights** (the greedy fails; dynamic programming takes over). ## Part A — Lessons ## A1. Representing intervals: open, closed and half-open ends {#sec-int-repr} ::: {.callout-note title="In plain words"} Every interval problem quietly picks a convention for its two ends. **Closed** $[a, b]$ includes both ends, so $[1,3]$ and $[3,5]$ share the point $3$. **Half-open** $[a, b)$ includes the start and excludes the end, so $[1,3)$ and $[3,5)$ are disjoint: a film that ends at $3$ and a film that starts at $3$ can both be watched. **Open** $(a, b)$ excludes both; it appears in geometry ("strictly inside") more than in scheduling. The convention is rarely named in the statement, and it decides what the code does when two ends sit at the same coordinate. ::: The three conventions, the membership test, and when two intervals overlap: ```text convention contains x [1,3]-type and [3,5]-type overlap test for (a1,b1), (a2,b2) [a, b] a <= x <= b share the point 3 a1 <= b2 and a2 <= b1 [a, b) a <= x < b disjoint a1 < b2 and a2 < b1 (a, b) a < x < b disjoint a1 < b2 and a2 < b1 (for a < b) ``` The overlap test reads "neither interval ends before the other starts". It is the only pairwise test the chapter needs, and every algorithm below is a way of *not* running it on all $\binom{n}{2}$ pairs. **Which statements use which.** LC 56 *Merge Intervals* says $[1,4]$ and $[4,5]$ overlap: closed. LC 1094 *Car Pooling* says passengers are dropped off before new ones are picked up at the same location: half-open. CSES 1629 *Movie Festival* has a sample whose answer needs a film to start at the moment the previous one ends: half-open. CSES 1619 *Restaurant Customers* sidesteps the question by promising that all times are distinct. When a statement says nothing, test a touching pair on the samples, or ask. **Integers make the choice reversible.** When the coordinates are integers (days, kilometre markers, array indices), a closed interval $[a, b]$ holds exactly the integers of the half-open interval $[a, b+1)$. So you can convert once, at input time, and write the rest of the code for one convention only. LC 986's event form (@sec-int-p5-a) does exactly this. **The tie-breaker follows from the convention.** Split each interval into an arrival event at $a$ and a departure event at $b$. When an arrival and a departure sit at the same coordinate $t$, the order in which you process them decides whether the two intervals count as overlapping at $t$: ```text half-open [a, b) the departing interval has already released t -> process the -1 FIRST closed [a, b] both intervals contain t -> process the +1 FIRST ``` That one decision is the difference between "two films fit" and "the room peaks at two". Get it wrong and a sweep reports a peak one too high or one too low, and only on inputs where ends touch, which is exactly where random tests rarely look. ::: {#fig-int-repr} ::: {#a6909c58 .cell renderings='["light","dark"]' execution_count=3} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](014_intervals_files/figure-html/cell-4-output-1.png){width=488 height=232} ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](014_intervals_files/figure-html/cell-4-output-2.png){width=488 height=232} ::: ::: The same two pairs of numbers under two conventions. Closed (green), both intervals contain $3$, so they overlap at one point and a sweep must count both there. Half-open (indigo, dashed), the first interval stops just before $3$, so the pair is disjoint. The counts on the right are computed from the membership tests above. ::: ::: {#arr-int-a1-demo .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} def overlap_closed(x, y): return x[0] <= y[1] and y[0] <= x[1] def overlap_half(x, y): return x[0] < y[1] and y[0] < x[1] def peak(intervals, tie_depart_first): """Sweep with the tie order as a parameter: True = half-open reading, False = closed.""" evs = sorted([(a, +1) for a, _ in intervals] + [(b, -1) for _, b in intervals], key=lambda e: (e[0], e[1] if tie_depart_first else -e[1])) cur = best = 0 for _, d in evs: cur += d best = max(best, cur) return best ivs = [(1, 3), (3, 5)] assert overlap_closed(*ivs) and not overlap_half(*ivs) assert peak(ivs, tie_depart_first=True) == 1 # half-open [a,b): they do NOT overlap assert peak(ivs, tie_depart_first=False) == 2 # closed [a,b]: they share 3 # On integers, closed [a, b] is half-open [a, b + 1): the two overlap tests agree after conversion. for _ in range(500): x = sorted(random.sample(range(12), 2)); y = sorted(random.sample(range(12), 2)) by_points = bool(set(range(x[0], x[1] + 1)) & set(range(y[0], y[1] + 1))) assert overlap_closed(x, y) == by_points == overlap_half((x[0], x[1] + 1), (y[0], y[1] + 1)) print("a1 demo OK") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` a1 demo OK ``` ::: ::: The two `peak` asserts *are* the lesson: same intervals, same $+1$/$-1$ events, only the tie order changes, and the reported peak moves from $1$ to $2$. The loop checks the integer conversion against the definition (a common integer point), so you may convert closed integer intervals to half-open ones and use one set of comparisons everywhere. ## A2. Merging and inserting intervals after sorting by start {#sec-int-merge} ::: {.callout-note title="In plain words"} To **merge** intervals into maximal non-overlapping blocks, do two things: **sort by start**, then walk with the end of the block you are building. Each next interval either starts inside that block, so the block's end becomes the larger of the two ends, or starts after it, so the block is finished and a new one opens. After the sort, an interval can only touch the *last* block, because every earlier block ended before the last one began. To **insert** one interval into a list that is already sorted and merged, skip the sort: copy the intervals strictly to the left, absorb the ones that overlap, copy the rest. ::: The merge template: ```text sort intervals by start out = [] for iv in intervals: if out and iv.start <= out[-1].end: # overlap or touch (closed); use < for half-open out[-1].end = max(out[-1].end, iv.end) # extend, never replace else: out.append(copy(iv)) # disjoint: open a new block ``` **Why sorting by start is enough.** After the sort, every unprocessed interval starts at or after the current one. So a block, once a later interval starts beyond its end, can never be touched again: everything still to come starts even later. That is the whole correctness argument, and it is why only `out[-1]` is ever examined. Two bugs to stamp out on day one. First, comparing `iv.start` with the *previous interval's* end instead of the *block's* end: on $[1,10],[2,3],[4,5]$ the previous interval of $[4,5]$ is $[2,3]$, the test $4 \le 3$ fails, and a second block opens although $[4,5]$ lies inside $[1,10]$ (@fig-int-nested draws it). Second, writing `out[-1].end = iv.end` instead of taking the `max`: the nested $[2,3]$ shrinks the block $[1,10]$ to $[1,3]$, and $[4,5]$ then opens a block of its own. ::: {#fig-int-anim-merge} ::: {#67c4a9f7 .cell execution_count=5} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
visit [1,3]: starts after the block: open a new one; blocks = [1,3]
visit [2,6]: starts inside the block: extend; blocks = [1,6]
visit [8,10]: starts after the block: open a new one; blocks = [1,6] [8,10]
visit [15,18]: starts after the block: open a new one; blocks = [1,6] [8,10] [15,18]
``` ::: ::: The merge walk on $[1,3],[8,10],[2,6],[15,18]$ after sorting by start. The amber bar is the interval being visited, dashed bars are still to come, and the green row under the axis is the block list. $[2,6]$ starts inside $[1,3]$ and extends it to $[1,6]$; $[8,10]$ and $[15,18]$ each start after the last block and open a new one. ::: ::: {#arr-int-a2-demo .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} def merge(intervals): out = [] for a, b in sorted(intervals): if out and a <= out[-1][1]: out[-1][1] = max(out[-1][1], b) else: out.append([a, b]) return out def insert(intervals, new): out, i, n = [], 0, len(intervals) while i < n and intervals[i][1] < new[0]: # strictly left out.append(list(intervals[i])); i += 1 cur = list(new) while i < n and intervals[i][0] <= cur[1]: # absorb overlaps cur = [min(cur[0], intervals[i][0]), max(cur[1], intervals[i][1])] i += 1 out.append(cur) while i < n: # strictly right out.append(list(intervals[i])); i += 1 return out def gaps(intervals): """The holes between merged blocks, as open stretches (b_k, a_{k+1}).""" m = merge(intervals) return [(m[k][1], m[k + 1][0]) for k in range(len(m) - 1)] def merge_brute(intervals): """Union-find over the overlap relation, then one block per component.""" n = len(intervals) parent = list(range(n)) def find(x): while parent[x] != x: parent[x] = parent[parent[x]] x = parent[x] return x for i in range(n): for j in range(i + 1, n): if overlap_closed(intervals[i], intervals[j]): parent[find(i)] = find(j) comp = {} for i, (a, b) in enumerate(intervals): r = find(i) lo, hi = comp.get(r, (a, b)) comp[r] = (min(lo, a), max(hi, b)) return sorted([list(x) for x in comp.values()]) assert merge([[1, 3], [8, 10], [2, 6], [15, 18]]) == [[1, 6], [8, 10], [15, 18]] assert merge([[1, 10], [2, 3], [4, 5]]) == [[1, 10]] # nested: the max() keeps the block assert insert([[1, 2], [3, 5], [6, 7], [8, 10], [12, 16]], [4, 8]) == [[1, 2], [3, 10], [12, 16]] assert gaps([[1, 3], [8, 10], [2, 6], [15, 18]]) == [(6, 8), (10, 15)] for _ in range(300): ivs = [sorted([random.randint(0, 20), random.randint(0, 20)]) for _ in range(random.randint(1, 12))] got = merge(ivs) assert got == merge_brute(ivs) new = sorted([random.randint(0, 20), random.randint(0, 20)]) assert insert(got, new) == merge(ivs + [new]) # insert = merge on a merged list print("a2 demo OK") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` a2 demo OK ``` ::: ::: The oracle `merge_brute` never sorts: it joins every overlapping *pair* (connected components of the overlap relation), so it is independent of the walk's reasoning. Agreement on random inputs confirms that "only the last block can be touched" is true. The second assert says that `insert` on a merged list is the same function as `merge` on the whole pile, only cheaper: once the input is sorted *and* merged, you can skip the sort and cut the list at two positions. And `gaps` shows the remark from the plain-words box: the holes of a family are the stretches between consecutive merged blocks, which @sec-int-p5-c counts. ## A3. Events: turning intervals into +1/−1 points and sweeping {#sec-int-events} ::: {.callout-note title="In plain words"} The most reusable idea of the chapter. Store an interval not as one bar but as **two events on a shared timeline**: at $a$, "one more interval is active"; at $b$, "one fewer". Sort all $2n$ events by position and walk them with a running count. Picture a vertical line, the **sweep line**, moving from left to right and stopping at every event: at each stop, the running count is exactly the number of intervals the line crosses. Nothing is ever compared with anything else; the order of the events does all the work. ::: The template: ```text events = [(start, +1) for each interval] + [(end, -1) for each interval] sort events by (position, tie_breaker) # tie_breaker from the convention (A1) cur = best = 0 for pos, delta in events: cur += delta # intervals crossing the sweep line just after pos best = max(best, cur) # or: record (pos, cur), compare with a capacity, ... ``` This is the **sparse difference array** of @sec-pref-diff. With small integer coordinates you can keep a plain array, `diff[a] += 1; diff[b + 1] -= 1` for closed intervals, and a prefix sum gives the count at every position; @sec-int-p2-b does exactly that. With coordinates up to $10^9$ the array is impossible, and sorting the $2n$ events visits only the positions where the count changes. A third option is to compress the coordinates first (@sec-srt-a4) and run the array on ranks, which @sec-int-p2-a shows. ::: {#fig-int-anim-sweep} ::: {#fc88185d .cell execution_count=7} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
t = 1: [1,5] starts, count +1 = 1, peak 1
t = 2: [2,6] starts, count +1 = 2, peak 2
t = 4: [4,8] starts, count +1 = 3, peak 3
t = 5: [1,5] ends, count -1 = 2, peak 3
t = 6: [2,6] ends, count -1 = 1, peak 3
t = 7: [7,9] starts, count +1 = 2, peak 3
t = 8: [4,8] ends, count -1 = 1, peak 3
t = 9: [7,9] ends, count -1 = 0, peak 3
``` ::: ::: The sweep line (dashed) stops at each of the eight events of four closed intervals. Green bars are crossed by the line, dashed bars have not started, grey bars are finished, and the amber bar is the one whose start or end the line just met. The count climbs to $3$ at $t = 4$, falls at $5$ and $6$, rises again at $7$ when $[7,9]$ starts while $[4,8]$ is still running, and returns to $0$. No two bars were ever compared. ::: **What the running count answers.** The same walk, with a different line inside the loop: - **Peak overlap**: the maximum of `cur`. - **Union length**: add `pos - prev` to a total whenever `cur > 0` on the stretch $[\text{prev}, \text{pos})$. - **Time above a capacity**, or the first moment the load exceeds it: compare `cur` with the capacity on each stretch. - **Points covered exactly $k$ times** (CF 1000C): add the length of each stretch to a bucket indexed by `cur`. **Rooms: the peak is also the number of rooms needed.** Suppose each interval is a meeting and you must give every meeting a room, with no two overlapping meetings in one room. At the peak moment, `best` meetings run at once, so at least `best` rooms are needed. And `best` rooms always suffice: walk the meetings by start and put each into any room that is already free (a min-heap of room end times finds one). A new room is opened only when every existing room is busy at this meeting's start, and then all those meetings plus this one cover that start point, so the number of rooms never exceeds the peak. This is the interval-partitioning theorem (Kleinberg–Tardos § 4.1), and Movie Festival II's oracle (@sec-int-p3-b) relies on it. **Point queries without a sweep.** For many questions "how many intervals contain $t$?", sort the starts into $S$ and the ends into $E$. A closed interval contains $t$ when it started at or before $t$ and has not ended before $t$, so the count is $|\{a \le t\}| - |\{b < t\}|$, two binary searches (@sec-bst-p1). For half-open intervals, use $|\{a \le t\}| - |\{b \le t\}|$. ::: {#arr-int-a3-demo .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} def max_overlap(intervals, half_open=True): """half_open: departures before arrivals at equal coordinates; closed: arrivals first.""" key = (lambda e: (e[0], e[1])) if half_open else (lambda e: (e[0], -e[1])) ev = sorted([(a, +1) for a, _ in intervals] + [(b, -1) for _, b in intervals], key=key) cur = best = 0 for _, d in ev: cur += d best = max(best, cur) return best def max_overlap_brute(intervals, half_open=True): inside = (lambda a, b, t: a <= t < b) if half_open else (lambda a, b, t: a <= t <= b) return max((sum(inside(a, b, t) for a, b in intervals) for t, _ in intervals), default=0) def union_length(intervals): """Total length covered at least once, by the sweep.""" ev = sorted([(a, +1) for a, _ in intervals] + [(b, -1) for _, b in intervals]) total, cur, prev = 0, 0, None for pos, d in ev: if cur > 0: total += pos - prev cur += d prev = pos return total def min_rooms(intervals): """Greedy room assignment for half-open meetings: reuse any room free by the start.""" ends = [] # min-heap of room end times for a, b in sorted(intervals): if ends and ends[0] <= a: heappop(ends) # that room is free again heappush(ends, b) return len(ends) def count_at(S, E, t, closed=True): """S, E: sorted starts and ends. Intervals containing t.""" return bisect.bisect_right(S, t) - (bisect.bisect_left(E, t) if closed else bisect.bisect_right(E, t)) assert max_overlap([(1, 3), (3, 5)], half_open=True) == 1 assert max_overlap([(1, 3), (3, 5)], half_open=False) == 2 assert max_overlap([(1, 5), (2, 6), (4, 8), (7, 9)], half_open=False) == 3 assert union_length([(1, 3), (2, 6), (8, 10)]) == 7 # [1,6] and [8,10] for _ in range(400): iv = [tuple(sorted(random.sample(range(16), 2))) for _ in range(random.randint(1, 7))] for ho in (True, False): assert max_overlap(iv, ho) == max_overlap_brute(iv, ho) assert union_length(iv) == sum(b - a for a, b in merge(iv)) assert min_rooms(iv) == max_overlap(iv, half_open=True) # rooms needed = peak S, E = sorted(a for a, _ in iv), sorted(b for _, b in iv) for t in range(16): assert count_at(S, E, t, closed=True) == sum(a <= t <= b for a, b in iv) assert count_at(S, E, t, closed=False) == sum(a <= t < b for a, b in iv) print("a3 demo OK") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` a3 demo OK ``` ::: ::: The stress test checks both conventions against an oracle that tests each candidate point directly (the peak is always reached at some start, so the starts are enough candidates). It also checks the union length against the merged blocks of A2, the room count against the peak, and the two-binary-search point count against the definition. Change the closed key `(e[0], -e[1])` into the half-open one and the closed assertion fails on inputs where an end meets a start: the A1 contract paying rent. ## A4. Greedy interval scheduling and covering: sort by end, sort by start {#sec-int-sched} ::: {.callout-note title="In plain words"} Three classic questions, three greedy rules. **Pack**: keep as many pairwise disjoint intervals as possible (films in one cinema, tasks on one machine). Sort by **end**, and take every interval that starts after the last one you took: the interval that ends first leaves the most room for the rest. **Stab**: find the fewest points such that every interval contains one (arrows through balloons). Sort by **end**, and place a point at the end of the first interval not yet hit: that point hits as many later intervals as any point could. **Cover**: choose the fewest intervals whose union contains a whole segment $[L, R]$ (clips of a video). Sort by **start**, and among the intervals that start inside the part already covered, take the one that reaches farthest. ::: The three templates side by side (closed intervals for stab and cover, half-open for pack, as in the problems that use them): ```text pack (activity selection) stab (fewest points) cover [L, R] (fewest intervals) sort by end sort by end sort by start last = -inf; count = 0 shot = -inf; arrows = 0 reach = L; count = 0; i = 0 for iv: for iv: while reach < R: if iv.start >= last: if iv.start > shot: best = reach count += 1 arrows += 1 while i < n and iv[i].start <= reach: last = iv.end shot = iv.end best = max(best, iv[i].end); i += 1 if best == reach: return -1 # a hole reach = best; count += 1 ``` **Why packing by earliest end is optimal ("greedy stays ahead").** Let the greedy take $g_1, g_2, \dots, g_k$ and let an optimal solution take $o_1, o_2, \dots, o_m$, both listed by end. Claim: $\text{end}(g_i) \le \text{end}(o_i)$ for every $i \le k$. For $i = 1$ the greedy took the interval with the smallest end of all. For $i > 1$, $o_i$ starts after $o_{i-1}$ ends, which is at or after $g_{i-1}$'s end by induction, so $o_i$ was still available when the greedy chose $g_i$, and the greedy chose the available interval with the smallest end. Now if $m > k$, the interval $o_{k+1}$ starts after $\text{end}(o_k) \ge \text{end}(g_k)$, so it was available after $g_k$ and the greedy would not have stopped. Hence $k \ge m$. The same argument in exchange form ("swap the optimal solution's first interval for the greedy's") is the one @sec-srt-a5 uses for orderings. **Why stabbing at the earliest end is optimal.** Some point must hit the interval $I_1$ with the smallest end $b_1$, and such a point lies at or before $b_1$. Slide it right to $b_1$: every interval it hit contains it and ends at or after $b_1$ (no end is smaller), so it still contains $b_1$. So some optimal solution shoots at $b_1$; remove what that shot hits and repeat. A bonus fact: for intervals, **the fewest stabbing points equals the most pairwise disjoint intervals**. No point can hit two disjoint intervals, so you need at least as many points as disjoint intervals; and the intervals that triggered the greedy's shots are pairwise disjoint (each starts after the previous shot), so the greedy achieves that bound. The demo below checks the equality. **Why covering by farthest reach is optimal.** After $c$ chosen intervals the greedy has covered $[L, \text{reach}]$, the longest prefix that any $c$ intervals can cover. The next interval of any solution must start inside the prefix covered so far, which is not longer than the greedy's, so it is among the candidates the greedy considered, and the greedy took the one reaching farthest. @sec-int-p4-c solves the problem. **The wrong greedies.** Each rule fails with the other sort, and the other "natural" rules fail too. Packing by earliest **start** takes one long interval and blocks many short ones (@fig-int-sched). Packing by **shortest** first fails on $[1,5],[4,7],[6,10]$: the short $[4,7]$ blocks both others, while $[1,5],[6,10]$ fit. Stabbing at the end of the earliest-**starting** interval fails on $[1,10],[2,3]$: the shot at $10$ misses $[2,3]$, while one shot at $3$ hits both. If you cannot state the exchange argument, suspect the greedy. ::: {#fig-int-sched} ::: {#20cfd857 .cell renderings='["light","dark"]' execution_count=9} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](014_intervals_files/figure-html/cell-10-output-1.png){width=453 height=367} ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](014_intervals_files/figure-html/cell-10-output-2.png){width=453 height=367} ::: ::: The packing greedy on the same four intervals in two orders. On a **circle** (hours of a day, positions around a round table) an interval may wrap past the cut, like a night shift $[22, 2)$; neither end is "earlier". On a **weighted** line every interval carries a value and you want the most valuable disjoint set, not the largest one. The first is repaired by cutting the circle and splitting the wrapping intervals in two; the second is not a greedy problem at all. ::: **Splitting at the cut.** Put the cut at $0$ on a circle of length $C$. A non-wrapping interval $[a, b)$ with $a < b$ stays as it is; a wrapping one ($a > b$, read clockwise from $a$ to $b$) becomes the two pieces $[a, C)$ and $[0, b)$. Every point of the circle lies in exactly one copy of the line $[0, C)$, and a point is covered by a wrapping interval exactly when it is covered by one of its two pieces. So any question about **coverage at points** (peak overlap, union length, free stretches) is answered exactly by running the linear sweep of @sec-int-events on the pieces. Questions about **choosing intervals** (pack, stab, cover) need more care, because a wrapping interval cut in two must not count as two intervals. The standard repair is to *unroll*: copy every interval shifted by $C$, so the line $[0, 2C)$ holds two laps, and run the linear greedy on a window of length $C$ starting at a chosen interval; trying each start costs $O(n)$ per start, and faster versions use binary lifting, which belongs to a later volume. ::: {#fig-int-circle} ::: {#d861a3e8 .cell renderings='["light","dark"]' execution_count=12} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](014_intervals_files/figure-html/cell-13-output-1.png){width=469 height=201} ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](014_intervals_files/figure-html/cell-13-output-2.png){width=469 height=201} ::: ::: Three half-open intervals on a circle of length $12$, cut open at $0$. Two intervals count as overlapping if they share at least one point, so $[1,3]$ and $[3,4]$ merge into $[1,4]$. This is @sec-srt's "sort first" purchase spent on the *merge* relation. The subtle bug that catches almost everyone is comparing an interval to the *previous original* end instead of the *current block* end; nested intervals like $[1,10],[2,3],[4,5]$ then shrink the block incorrectly. ::: ::: {.p-approach} 1. **Pairwise passes until stable.** Repeatedly scan for any overlapping pair, merge that pair, and restart. Correct by definition, $O(n^3)$ worst case — the oracle. 2. **Sort by start, then a stack of blocks.** Sort once; walk with a stack whose top is the block currently being grown. Extend the top when the next interval overlaps, push a new block otherwise. $O(n\log n)$, $O(n)$ extra space (the stack). 3. **Sort by start, then a running end.** Same walk, but the "stack" has been collapsed into a `out[-1][1]` cell because the only block you ever modify is the last one. $O(n\log n)$ time, $O(n)$ for the output (in-place variant is $O(1)$ extra). **Invariant.** `out` is a list of disjoint, maximally-merged blocks over `intervals[:k+1]`, sorted by start. The result is a three-phase linear walk: **copy-left, absorb-overlaps, copy-right**. You sort intervals in C++ with the comparator `return a[0] <= b[0];`. What can go wrong?** ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"} `std::sort` requires a strict weak ordering, and `<=` is not irreflexive (an element compares less than itself), so the behaviour is undefined: in practice wrong orders, or reads past the end of the array on some inputs. Use `<`, or for several keys compare the first key and fall back to the second, as in `a[0] != b[0] ? a[0] < b[0] : a[1] > b[1]` (@sec-srt-a2). ::: **13. Can the maximum overlap of $n$ intervals be computed faster than $O(n\log n)$ in the comparison model?** ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"} Not in general. Deciding whether some two numbers among $x_1, \dots, x_n$ are equal (element distinctness) needs $\Omega(n\log n)$ comparisons in the algebraic decision-tree model, and it reduces to the overlap question: the closed point-intervals $[x_i, x_i]$ have peak overlap $\ge 2$ exactly when two numbers are equal. With small integer coordinates the difference array beats the bound, because it uses the values as addresses, not comparisons (@sec-pref-diff). ::: ## Summary ::: {.callout-important title="Templates to remember"} - **Convention first:** closed $[a,b]$ overlap test `a1 <= b2 and a2 <= b1`; half-open `a1 < b2 and a2 < b1`; on integers $[a,b] = [a, b+1)$. Sweep ties: half-open processes $-1$ first, closed $+1$ first (@sec-int-repr). - **Merge:** sort by start; extend the last block with `max(out[-1].end, iv.end)` or open a new one (@sec-int-merge, @sec-int-p1-a). - **Insert into a merged list:** copy strictly-left, absorb overlaps, copy the rest; no sort (@sec-int-p1-b). - **Event sweep:** $(a, +w)$ and $(b, -w)$, sort with the convention's tie-break, running sum: peak, capacity check, union length, rooms $=$ peak (@sec-int-events, @sec-int-p2). - **Pack:** sort by end; take each interval that starts at or after the last end; $k$ resources: best-fit multiset of free times (@sec-int-p3). - **Stab:** sort by end; shoot at the end of each interval not yet hit; fewest points $=$ most disjoint intervals (@sec-int-p4-a). - **Containment:** sort by (start asc, end desc); covered iff `end <= max_end` (@sec-int-p4-b). - **Cover $[0,T]$:** sort by start; each round take the farthest end among intervals starting inside the covered prefix; no progress means a hole (@sec-int-p4-c). - **Intersect:** two lists, two pointers, advance the smaller end; a family, $[\max l, \min r]$ (@sec-int-p5-a, @sec-int-p5-b). - **Gaps:** sort by start, running reach; a start beyond `reach + 1` (integer days) opens a gap (@sec-int-p5-c). ::: - Nearly every interval problem is one sort plus one walk; the walk keeps one small piece of state (a block end, a count, a free time, a reach, two cursors) that the sort makes sufficient (@sec-int-p1 to @sec-int-p5). - The endpoint convention is part of the problem, not a detail: it fixes the overlap test, the sweep's tie order and the strictness of every greedy comparison, and it only shows on touching inputs, so test those on purpose (@sec-int-repr). - The event sweep is the difference array without the array; it answers every question about *how many* intervals cover a point, and the peak it finds is also the number of rooms needed (@sec-int-events). - Sort by **start** to build or scan the union (merge, cover, gaps, room assignment); sort by **end** to choose intervals (pack, stab, $k$-resource scheduling). Each greedy has a short exchange or "stays ahead" proof, and each fails under the other sort (@sec-int-sched). - The fewest points stabbing all intervals equals the most pairwise disjoint intervals: one greedy computes both (@sec-int-sched). - Several resources are not several runs of the one-resource greedy: assign each interval to the resource that became free latest but in time (@sec-int-p3-b). - Two sorted interval lists intersect in linear time with two pointers; a whole family intersects in one pass with $[\max l, \min r]$ (@sec-int-p5). - Circles reduce to lines by a split (coverage) or by unrolling (choice); weights end the greedy and start the DP (@sec-int-circle). ## Practice ladder Ordered by concept, following the patterns.
